2. Writ petitioners challenged the purported actions of eviction by the appellants from holding No. 572 appertaining to CS Plot Nos. 434, 435 and 436 corresponding to RS Khatian No. 1145 of RS plot Nos. 651 and 653 of Mouza Joarshahara, Dhaka Cantonment in the High Court Division by a writ petition. According to the writ petitioners, by different deeds they acquired title and possession of 0.6855 acre of land out of the aforesaid three plots and constructed four multistoried buildings under the name 'Chowdhury Kunjo'. It is stated that a portion of those three plots were acquired by the Government in 1951 in LA Case No. 32A of 19494950 and thereafter it exchanged the acquired land with the Military Estate Department, and the later included the same in the Kurmitola cantonment. There was a public announcement on 27th January, 2007 in the locality that the writ petitioners would be evicted from that property by demolishing the constructions. 

 3. Appellants contested the petition claiming that the writ petitioners constructed the buildings by encroaching the land of Military Estate Department which it had exchanged with the Government and became the absolute owner. The writ petitioners violating the layout plan of the RAJUK made constructions on the disputed land and despite issuance of notices for removal of the unauthorized constructions, the writ petitioners neglected the said notices and as a result, the RAJUK cancelled the plan for construction of the buildings. 

 4. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties by the impugned judgment disposed of the rule holding that the writ petitioners and the Military Estate Department are 'co-owners' in CS Plot Nos. 434, 435 and 436, that unless the lands are demarcated between the co-owners each co-owner can claim ownership on every inch of land like a co-sharer, that the demarcation of the plots should be made by a properly constituted partition suit and until the lands are partitioned by metes and bounds, the appellants cannot interfere with the possession of the writ petitioners. 

 b) the disputed land comprised in CS Plot Nos. 434, 435 and 436 was admittedly acquired and vested in the Government in LA. Case No. 324/49-50 and the Military Estate Department admittedly is in possession of the said land and that the acquired land vests absolutely free from all encumbrances and all interest/share in the land stand extinguished and ceased to exist and as such, previous land owners do not and cannot retain any particular interest in any unit of the land acquired and thus the High Court Division proceeded on irrational, illogical, illegal and ultra vires premise of portability of acquired vested land and so erred in law in directing the appellants to resort to partition suit for recovery of encroached acquired land. 

 d) the High Court Division committed gross error of law in holding that the Military Estate Department became a co-owner with the writ petitioners in respect of CS Plot Nos. 334, 335 and 336 in holding that the status of co-owner and the co-sharer is the same so far demarcation of land is concerned and further in holding that the co-owner of the land have title on every inch of the entire land till co-owner is given its separate demarcated quantum of land." 

 8. Admittedly CS Plot Nos. 434, 435 and 436 measuring an area of 4.2 acres have been acquired by the Government under the (Emergency) Requisition of property Act, 1948 and thereafter, the said lands were exchanged with the Military Estate Department with other lands and since the date of exchange the Military Estate Department has been enjoying the said lands. As soon as a piece of land is acquired by the Government, the acquired land absolutely vests in the Government free from all encumbrances. Learned Counsel for the writ petitioners did not dispute the power of the RAJUK or the Military Estate Department to remove unauthorized constructions. His main contention is that the boundary of the lands of the writ petitioners and the appellants having not been demarcated, it cannot be said that the writ petitioners have constructed the buildings by encroaching the land of the appellants. Alternatively, learned Counsel submits that the appellants have to show that which portion of the land has been encroached by the writ petitioners. Since the acquisition of lands out of the three plots is vague without specifying the boundary, learned counsel submits, it cannot be said that the Writ Petitioners have constructed buildings encroaching on the appellants land. 

 9. The moot question is whether the appellants can remove the unauthorized constructions without demarcation of lands by metes and bounds as claimed. Section 5(7) of Act of 1948 provides that after performing formalities, on and from the day of publication of a notice in the Official Gazette to the effect that the Government has decided to acquire the land, the requisitioned land absolutely vests in the Government free from all encumbrances. In this case the Gazette Notification under section 5 (7) of the Act was published on 31st May, 1951, when the property vested in the Government and since then whatever right the ex-owners had in the said three plots in respect of acquired portion of land ceased to exist. Neither the ex-owners nor any person claiming under them can claim any right or interest whatsoever in the acquired land. The acquisition of title and interest by a private individual and that of the Government is completely distinct. The expression 'vest' means to give an immediate, fixed right of present and future enjoyment; to accrue to; to be fixed; to take effect; to clothe with possession; to deliver full possession of land or of an estate. 

 10. In Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, 4th Edn, the word 'vested' has been defined in several senses it is stated: 

 14. The High Court Division has totally misconstrued the expression 'co-owner' and made the above observations. The term 'joint owners' embraces all cases where the property in question is owned by two or more persons regardless of the special nature of their relationship or how it came into being. This expression is synonymous to co-owner. A co-owner means who is in concurrent ownership, possession and enjoyment of property with one or more others. The writ petitioners did not claim that they are in joint possession or co-ownership of the disputed land with the Military Estate Department. Their positive case is that Subedar Md Giasuddin Chowdhury purchased the lands by different deeds, mutated his name, paid rent to the Government and with buildings. These admitted facts proved that the writ petitioners are not in joint possession with the Military Estate Department and therefore, under no stretch of imagination it can be said that they are 'co-owners' with Military Estate Department in respect of those three plots. 

 15. If a record of right is changed by way of mutation in accordance with the procedure provided in section 117(1)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by a competent authority and if such mutation is effected by payment of rent, then with such separation from a joint holding other co-sharers ceased to be co-sharers. The effect of separation of a share from the joint holding falls upon all co-sharers of the original holding. It has been held by this Division in Md. Khairullal Bhuiyan vs Hazi Nurul Alam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 338, Separation necessarily means sub-division of a joint tenancy and falls under and is governed by clause (c) of section 117. "Effect of separation of a share from the joint holding falls upon all the co-sharers who, after separation, cease to be co-shares of the original holding "A co-sharer after getting his share separated may his portion constituted into a new tenancy or he may tag this share with his other land, if any, and if he does so, his case may be referred to as a case of 'separation and amalgamation' for the sake of convenience, though the two terms are quite different." Separation of jama of sub-division of a holding or tenancy distributing rents, whether in case of agricultural land or non-agricultural land takes place under section 117(1)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The original co-sharers on such separation cease to be co-sharers. 

 16. Thus the writ petitioners are neither co-owners nor co-sharers of the disputed plots. They have mutated their names in Mutation Case No. 19588 of 2001 on 3rd December, 2001 which is apparent from the khatian. The High Court Division over looked the same and on a misconception of law termed them as co-owners. The High Court Division though noticed that land purchased by the writ petitioners had already recorded in their names in SA and RS records, on misconception of law held that the Military Estate Department is a co-owner. This finding of the High Court Division is misconceived one, inasmuch as, if the writ petitioners have mutated their names after purchase and separated khatians in respect of their lands, how they remain as co-owners or co-sharers is not known to us? The writ petitioners are exclusively claiming title on their purchased land and under no stretch of imagination they can he said as co-owners with Military Estate Department in respect of the three CS Plots. 

 17. Since the writ petitioners are not 'co-owners' of the disputed property with the Military Estate Department, the High Court Division on a misconception of law treated the writ petitioners as co-owners. Before the writ petitioner No. 1 had acquired title in a portion of CS plot Nos. 434, 435 and 436, his predecessors ceased any right in respect of acquired land as soon as Gazette Notification for acquisition was issued on 31st May, 1951. Secondly, after the writ petitioner No. 1 mutated his name and a new khatian was prepared in his name being RS Khatian No. 1145, he cannot claim as co-sharer of CS Khatian No. 304 of CS Plot numbers 434, and 435 and 436. Since the writ petitioners are not co-owners or co-sharers of the disputed plots, there is no legal bar to evicting the unauthorized occupants under section 5 of the Government and Local Authority Lands and Buildings (Recovery of Possession) Ordinance, 1970. The High Court Division erred therefore, in holding that the writ petitioners are not unauthorized occupants within the meaning of the Ordinance, 1970. 

 18. As soon as a piece of land is acquired in accordance with law the owner is deprived of his right. A citizen holds his property subject always to the right of the sovereign to take it for a public purpose. This right is called eminent domain. The right of eminent domain is the right of the sovereign State through its regular agencies. In Aiyar's Law Lexicon, Reprint Edn 1987, at page 387 the expression 'eminent domain' has been defined as under: "The right of the State or the sovereign to its or his own property is absolute while that of the subject or citizen to his property is only paramount. The citizen holds his property subject always to the right of the sovereign to take it for a public purpose  This right is called eminent domain 

 "The power to take private property for public use by the State, municipalities, and private persons or corporations authorized to exercise functions of public character In the United States, the power of eminent domain is founded in both the Federal (Fifth Amendment) and state constructions. The Construction limits the power to taking for a public purpose and prohibits the exercise of the power of eminent domain without just compensation to the owners of the property which is taken. The process of exercising the power of eminent domain is commonly referred to as 'condemnation' or 'expropriation." 

 20. In Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar vs State of Gujarat , 1995 Supp (1) SCC 596, K Ramaswamy, J argued in this connection as under: 

 "The right of eminent domain is the right of the sovereign State, through its regular agencies, to reassert, either temporarily or permanently, its dominion over any portion of the soil of the State including private property without its owner's consent on account of public exigency and for the public good. Eminent domain is the highest and most exact idea of property remaining in the Government, or in the aggregate body of the people in their sovereign capacity. It gives the right to resume possession of the property in the manner directed by the Constitution and the laws of the State, whenever the public interest requires it. The term 'expropriation' is practically synonymous with the term 'eminent domain". 

 23. In its affidavit-in-opposition in paragraph 9 RAJUK stated that the Authorized Officer 3 issued notice upon the Writ-Petitioner No. 1 Subeder Md Gias Uddin Chowdhury to remove unauthorized constructions on 24th June 2008 pointing out that he had been making constructions in violation of section 3 of the Building Construction Act, 1952. The appellants filed the said notice in their additional paper book filed on 8th May, 2011. Prior to that similar notice was issued on 24th January, 2004. Thereafter, the RAJUK cancelled the approved plan by its letter under memo dated 8th July 2008. It is contended that the cancellation of plan was done during the pendency of the writ petition. True, this notice was served during the pendency of the matter in the High Court Division but long before filing of the writ petition, RAJUK served two notices in 2004 for removal of unauthorized constructions but the writ petitioners ignoring the notices completed the constructions. Therefore, the statements in the writ petition that the direction for demolition was made without service of notice are contrary to the materials on record. 

 24. The High Court Division also found that the writ petitioners constructed the buildings beyond the approved plan which is evident from its observations that "albeit in a deviated manner". The High Court Division is of the view that since families have been possessing in the disputed buildings by purchase from the writ petitioners, who have no knowledge about the chequered history of the property and their interest cannot be affected, who are bona fide purchasers for value without notice. There is fallacy in the arguments of the High Court Division. If the writ petitioners have constructed the buildings by encroaching upon the lands of Military Estate Department who are none but trespassers, how then the purchasers from such trespassers, can claim better right in the said property? Despite such observation the High Court Division is of the view that the appellants cannot evict the writ petitioners as they are not "unauthorized occupants" within the meaning of section 2 (f) of the Government and Local Government Lands and Buildings (Recovery of Possession) Ordinance, 1970. 

 29. The High Court Division observed that there is dispute as to the exact location of the acquired land and the land owned and possessed by the writ petitioners and for ascertaining the area of land constituted a committee for measurement of their respective lands. The said committee submitted a report stating that though the writ petitioners have title and possession in respect of 0.5975 acre of land, in fact they are in possession in respect of 1.17815 acre and, therefore, they are in possession of excess land of 0.58065 acre. The High Court Division discarded the said report on the reasoning that the committee measured the land without ascertaining a fixed point. As observed above, the High Court Division was convinced that the writ petitioners are in possession of excess land and constructed the buildings encroaching upon the Military Estate Department's land and accordingly made a gratuitous observation that the (appellants) "may consider the change of the western alignment of the proposed road after the CS plot No. 433 towards the western part of the land which is the land owned by Military Estate Department or in the alternative to acquire the petitioners land in order to facilitate the construction of the said road in its present alignment." This observation and order of injunction is beyond the scope of relief sought in the writ petition. Further, the question of acquisition of writ petitioners' land does not arise since there is positive claim of the appellant that writ petitioners have constructed the buildings on encroachment of Government land. 

 30. What is more, the High Court Division acted illegally in entering into the disputed questions of fact in ascertaining the quantum of land possessed by the writ petitioners and the appellants RAJUK in its affidavit-in-opposition clearly stated that the writ petitioners constructed three buildings violating the lay out plan and they were served with notice. When the writ petitioners were asked by notices to stop the constructions on the ground that they were making constructions encroaching upon land of the Government, they instituted title suit No. 324 of 1999. Since disputed questions of fact raised in the writ petition and since the writ petitioners had already instituted a Suit, this dispute could have been disposed of adequately in that suit. The writ petitioners had withdrawn their suit during the pendency of the writ petition and proceeded with petition at their risk and peril. 

 32. In view of the above, we find merit in the contention of the learned counsel for the appellants. The writ petitioners are not entitled to seek any relief from a Court of law for their unauthorized acts. The High Court Division has ignored that aspect of the matter and given reliefs to the petitioners despite finding that they have constructed the buildings by encroaching upon the land of the Military Estate Department. In view of above we find merit in these appeals.
